query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A single tailored thermo‐mechanical treatment—specifically a cryo‐rolling step followed by controlled annealing—can refine the as-cast lamellar structure of eutectic high-entropy alloys, producing an ultrafine hierarchical duplex microstructure that simultaneously enhances strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with inherently coarse lamellar fcc/B2 phases
generation.intervention: Apply severe cryo-rolling (inducing high plastic strain) immediately after casting followed by a controlled annealing process (at an optimized temperature, e.g., around 600°C) to activate phase-selective recrystallization and refine the microstructure
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing and quasi-static deformation; similar alloy composition and processing environment as in typical EHEA systems; processing parameters must maintain the lamellar nature while refining grain size
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine hierarchical duplex microstructure in which retained lamellar features coexist with recrystallized fine grains at phase boundaries
generation.mechanism: The intervention induces a two-hierarchical constraint effect where refined grains and preserved lamellae act synergistically: refined grain boundaries hinder dislocation motion (strengthening) while the inherited lamellae and phase interfaces better distribute strain and arrest microcrack propagation (enhancing ductility)
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast state, the treated alloy should show a significant increase in yield strength and an improvement in elongation-to-failure—yielding a higher strength–ductility synergy
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic HEA, which typically exhibits limited ductility and lower strength due to coarse lamellar microstructures
generation.boundary: This strategy is expected to be effective primarily in eutectic HEAs with a dual-phase lamellar (e.g., fcc/B2) structure; deviations in rolling strain, annealing temperature, or alloy chemistry may not produce the desired duplex refinement
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of improvement in strength and ductility depends on the fine-tuning of processing parameters and may vary with alloy composition; further optimization studies are needed

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA samples: one set remaining in the as-cast state and one set subjected to cryo-rolling (targeting a high strain, e.g., ~90% reduction) followed by controlled annealing at the optimized temperature (around 600°C for a fixed duration). Characterize each set using microscopy (SEM/TEM) to assess grain and lamellar refinement and perform room-temperature tensile tests to measure yield strength and ductility.
measurements: Grain size distribution and phase morphology via SEM/TEM
Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength from stress–strain curves
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cryo-rolled and annealed samples do not show a statistically significant increase in both yield strength and ductility (compared to the as-cast control) or if the expected ultrafine duplex hierarchical microstructure is not observed, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text:
A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
